subject: English Language
source: CISCE ICSE English Language (Paper 1) 2018 - Analysis of Pupil Performance (raw/LangPPA-18.pdf)

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (350 - 400 words) on the following:
Write an original short story entitled 'The Gift'.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: The story must be original and must bring out the theme of a special or meaningful gift. The giver and receiver should be the main characters.
key_points: Original story
Brings out the theme of a special or meaningful gift
The giver and receiver are the main characters
common_errors: Described the gift instead of its impact on the receiver
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many wrote a narrative instead of a story; ideas were borrowed from films and books. Some wrote of 'nature' or 'life' as gifts. The gift's impact on the receiver was often missing, with focus shifting to describing the gift.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (350 - 400 words) on the following:
"Money is important for happiness." Express your views either for or against this statement.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Argumentative essay: views for or against the motion are to be accepted. Credit is to be given for a cohesive, well-constructed, logical argument and ideas and reasoning based on personal experience. Candidate must take a clear stand and give valid reasons for the stand taken.
key_points: Takes one clear stand, either for or against
Valid reasons for the stand
Cohesive, logical argument drawing on reasoning and personal experience
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: The most popular topic. Many argued both sides without a clear stand; some essays became narratives with repeated points and no logic. A striking error was inserting short stories to illustrate points.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (350 - 400 words) on the following:
Narrate an incident from your own experience when you helped to prepare a meal. Explain what you did and what you gained from the experience.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Candidate should give clear sequencing of events, the effort involved, assistance given, result of effort and the lesson learnt. It must be a first-person account. 'I' is the central theme.
key_points: First-person account with 'I' at the centre
Clear sequence of events
The effort involved and assistance given
Result of the effort
The lesson learnt
common_errors: Group effort instead of personal role
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many did not say what help they gave, how, or to whom. Some described a group effort instead of their own part; some described help given to them by parents and siblings.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (350 - 400 words) on the following:
You had been waiting outside the examination hall. Describe what you saw and the sounds you heard when you arrived at the place. What were your feelings? Describe how the scene changed once you entered the hall and the examination started.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: A description of noise, chatter of children, parents, last minute rush to look at notes, etc. Teachers trying to solve doubts, give answers, telling them to relax. Parents asked to leave - the bell. The hush of the hall, prayer, silence, the examination begins.
key_points: Scene outside: noise, chatter of children and parents, last-minute rush to look at notes
Teachers solving doubts, telling students to relax
The narrator's feelings
Parents asked to leave; the bell
Change inside: the hush of the hall, prayer, silence, the examination begins
common_errors: Contrast with the silent hall missing
Dwelt on exam fear instead of the scene
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many skimmed over the scene outside the hall and did not draw on personal experience. Noise, chatter, last-minute rush and the silence inside were not focused on; some dwelt on exam fear from the previous night.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (350 - 400 words) on the following:
Study the picture given below. Write a story or a description or an account of what it suggests to you. Your composition may be about the subject of the picture or you may take suggestions from it; however, there must be a clear connection between the picture and your composition.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Picture Composition: Accept a wide interpretation. Any relevant ideas taken from the picture should be accepted. However, a mere itemization / listing / description of the picture is to be penalized.
key_points: Clear connection between the picture and the composition
Wide interpretation accepted: story, description or account
Not a mere itemisation/listing/description of the picture
common_errors: General essay on women's cricket/empowerment without the picture
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many wrote on women's cricket in India or on the girl child and women's empowerment without reference to the picture. Endings were often illogical; the link with the picture was missing as many strayed from its central theme.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation
penalised: Mere itemisation / listing / description of the picture

marking_schemes.question_text: Your uncle has offered to get you a pet for your birthday. Write a letter to him telling him what you would like, give reasons for your choice and tell him how you would take care of your pet.
marking_schemes.scheme_text:
Format (Friendly/Informal letter)
Content
Name the animal (it must be an animal, not a toy or gadget): e.g. cat / dog / turtle / gold fish
Reasons: e.g. unique / loving / easy to care for / no one has, or everyone else has / I am an animal lover / we have the space (Any two)
Care: e.g. cleaning / diet / health / walk / visit to vet / brushing / exercise / training (Any two)
Expression: criteria not itemised in the 2018 scheme.
Format (as printed in the 2018 scheme) - Informal letter: Address, Date, Salutation, Subscription, First name. Formal letter: From address, Date, To address, Salutation, Subscription, Name + surname / initial.
key_points: Correct informal letter format
Name the animal (it must be an animal, not a toy or gadget): e.g. cat / dog / turtle / gold fish
Reasons (any two): e.g. unique / loving / easy to care for / no one has, or everyone else has / I am an animal lover / we have the space
Care (any two): e.g. cleaning / diet / health / walk / visit to vet / brushing / exercise / training
Expression: criteria not itemised in the 2018 scheme.
common_errors: Thanked for a pet already received
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Format: incorrect and mixed formats; address in block letters; 'Respected uncle', 'Mamaji' in the salutation; 'XYZ' as signature. Content: many gave no reasons for wanting the pet, merged reason and care into one sentence, described the pet, or thanked the uncle for a pet already received.

format_elements: Date (day, month written in full, year)
Salutation addressing the recipient by name or relation (e.g. Dear Riya / Dear Grandma)
Body: opening sentence, content paragraphs, closing sentence
Subscription (e.g. Yours lovingly / Yours affectionately), no apostrophe in 'Yours'

content_requirements.element: Name the animal (it must be an animal, not a toy or gadget)

examples: no one has, or everyone else has

writing_task.expression_criteria: criteria not itemised in the 2018 scheme.

marking_schemes.question_text: The traffic outside your school is very heavy and chaotic. Write a letter to the Deputy Commissioner of Police (Traffic) pointing out the danger of such heavy and chaotic traffic in a school zone. Suggest possible solutions for the problem.
marking_schemes.scheme_text:
Format (Formal letter)
Content
Danger (should be explained): e.g. accident / death / no space to walk / jostling / misbehaviour / road rage / late to school (Any two)
Solutions: e.g. no parking / one way / patrol by police / school safety brigade / carpooling / school buses / encourage cycling or walking to school (Any two)
Expression: criteria not itemised in the 2018 scheme.
Format (as printed in the 2018 scheme) - Informal letter: Address, Date, Salutation, Subscription, First name. Formal letter: From address, Date, To address, Salutation, Subscription, Name + surname / initial.
key_points: Correct formal letter format
Danger (should be explained) (any two): e.g. accident / death / no space to walk / jostling / misbehaviour / road rage / late to school
Solutions (any two): e.g. no parking / one way / patrol by police / school safety brigade / carpooling / school buses / encourage cycling or walking to school
Expression: criteria not itemised in the 2018 scheme.
common_errors: Honking distraction given as the danger
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Format was often incorrect or incomplete. Content lacked analysis; many did not specify the danger, or treated distraction from honking as the danger.

format_elements: Date (day, month written in full, year)
Receiver's address beginning with the designation, then organisation and city
Salutation (Sir / Madam / Dear Sir / Dear Madam), not 'Respected Sir'
Body: opening sentence, content paragraphs, closing sentence

examples: encourage cycling or walking to school

accepted_alternatives: broken
worn out

stimulus.text:
Granny knew I'd been in the train for two nights, and she had a huge breakfast ready for me.

Later she told me there'd been a letter from Uncle Ken.

'He says he's the manager in Firpo's hotel in Simla,' she said. 'The salary is very good. It's a steady job and I hope he keeps it.'

Three days later Uncle Ken was on the veranda steps with his bedding roll and battered suitcase.

'Have you given up the hotel job?' asked Granny.

'No,' said Uncle Ken. 'They have closed down.'

'I hope it wasn't because of you.'

'No, Aunt Ellen. The bigger hotels in the hill stations are closing down.'

'Well, never mind. Come along and have your lunch.'

Over lunch, Uncle Ken talked very seriously about ways and means of earning a living.

'There is only one taxi in the whole of Dehra,' he mused. 'Surely there is business for another?'

'I'm sure there is,' said Granny. 'But where does it get you? In the first place, you don't have a taxi. And in the second place, you can't drive.'

'I can soon learn. There's a driving school in town. And I can use Uncle's old car.'

'I don't think it will run now,' said Granny.

'Of course, it will. It just needs some oiling and greasing and a spot of paint.'

'All right, learn to drive.'

So, Uncle Ken joined the driving school.

After a month Uncle Ken announced that he could drive and that he was taking the car out for a trial run.

'You haven't got your license yet,' said Granny.

'Oh, I won't take it far,' said Uncle Ken. 'Just down the road and back again.'

He spent all morning cleaning up the car. Granny gave him money for a can of petrol.

After tea, Uncle Ken said, 'Come along, Ruskin, hop in and I will give you a ride. Bring Mohan along too.' Mohan and I needed no urging. We got into the car beside Uncle Ken.

'Now don't go too fast, Ken,' said Granny anxiously. 'You are not used to the car as yet.'

Uncle Ken nodded and smiled and gave two sharp toots on the horn. He was feeling pleased with himself.

Driving through the gate, he nearly ran over a cat.

Miss Kellner, coming out for her evening rickshaw ride, saw Uncle Ken at the wheel of the car and ran indoors again.

Uncle Ken drove straight and fast, tootling the horn without a break.

At the end of the road there was a roundabout.

'We'll turn here,' said Uncle Ken, 'and then drive back again.'

He turned the steering wheel, we began going round the roundabout, but the steering wheel wouldn't turn all the way, not as much as Uncle Ken would have liked it to... So, instead he went on - and straight through the Maharaja of Jetpur's garden wall.

It was a single-brick wall, and the car knocked it down and emerged on the other side without any damage to the car or any of its occupants. Uncle Ken brought it to a halt in the middle of the Maharaja's lawn.

Running across the grass came the Maharaja himself. When he saw that it was Uncle Ken at the wheel, the Maharaja beamed with pleasure.

'Delighted to see you, old chap!' he exclaimed. 'Jolly decent of you to drop in again. How about a game of tennis?'
stimulus.source: Adapted from a Ruskin Bond story featuring Uncle Ken (source not printed in the PPA)
stimulus.line_references: Line numbers in questions refer to the printed paper's margin numbering.

marking_schemes.question_text: (ii) When Uncle Ken arrived with his luggage, Granny remarked that she hoped the hotel had not closed down because of him. What does this remark tell you about Uncle Ken?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: This is a critical thinking question - plausible answers to be accepted. Uncle Ken was constantly changing jobs / was not a steady person / irresponsible / eccentric (implied meaning to be accepted).
key_points: A plausible inference such as: he kept changing jobs / was not steady / irresponsible / eccentric (implied meaning accepted)
marking_schemes.model_answer: It suggests that Uncle Ken was not a steady person; he kept changing jobs and was irresponsible, so trouble often followed him.
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Needed critical thinking; many faltered and answers were wide and varied.

'I'm sure there is,' said Granny. 'But where does it get you? In the first place, you don't have a taxi. And in the second place, you can't drive.'

'I can soon learn. There's a driving school in town. And I can use Uncle's old car.'

'I don't think it will run now,' said Granny.

'Of course, it will. It just needs some oiling and greasing and a spot of paint.'

'All right, learn to drive.'

So, Uncle Ken joined the driving school.

After a month Uncle Ken announced that he could drive and that he was taking the car out for a trial run.

'You haven't got your license yet,' said Granny.

'Oh, I won't take it far,' said Uncle Ken. 'Just down the road and back again.'

He spent all morning cleaning up the car. Granny gave him money for a can of petrol.

After tea, Uncle Ken said, 'Come along, Ruskin, hop in and I will give you a ride. Bring Mohan along too.' Mohan and I needed no urging. We got into the car beside Uncle Ken.

'Now don't go too fast, Ken,' said Granny anxiously. 'You are not used to the car as yet.'

Uncle Ken nodded and smiled and gave two sharp toots on the horn. He was feeling pleased with himself.

Driving through the gate, he nearly ran over a cat.

Miss Kellner, coming out for her evening rickshaw ride, saw Uncle Ken at the wheel of the car and ran indoors again.

Uncle Ken drove straight and fast, tootling the horn without a break.

At the end of the road there was a roundabout.

'We'll turn here,' said Uncle Ken, 'and then drive back again.'

He turned the steering wheel, we began going round the roundabout, but the steering wheel wouldn't turn all the way, not as much as Uncle Ken would have liked it to... So, instead he went on - and straight through the Maharaja of Jetpur's garden wall.

It was a single-brick wall, and the car knocked it down and emerged on the other side without any damage to the car or any of its occupants. Uncle Ken brought it to a halt in the middle of the Maharaja's lawn.

Running across the grass came the Maharaja himself. When he saw that it was Uncle Ken at the wheel, the Maharaja beamed with pleasure.

'Delighted to see you, old chap!' he exclaimed. 'Jolly decent of you to drop in again. How about a game of tennis?'

paper_structure_note: 2018 paper: four questions - Q1 Composition [25] (350-400 words, 35 minutes), Q2 Letter [10], Q3 Comprehension [25], Q4 Grammar [20]. No notice/email question.

1: Explain the difference between a story and a narrative; mind-map to avoid repetition
Teach cohesive argument; do not accept stories in argumentative essays
Teach descriptive essays: senses, evocative imagery, figures of speech
Link the essay with the picture
2: Teach correct formal and informal formats
Discourage 'Examination Hall' as an address and 'XYZ' as a signature
Write in paragraphs; address the issue directly
3: Answer critical and analytical questions; note key words
Identify key nouns and verbs; write the summary in brief complete sentences
The title is for the summary, not the passage; justify it briefly
4: Practise mixed tenses in sentences and paragraphs
Use newspaper cuttings for preposition practice
Teach neither...nor; why 'still' and 'despite' are not used together

difficult_topics: Q1: interpretation of 'gifts'; equating money with happiness; taking a clear stand; narrative vs descriptive
Q2: format of formal and informal letters
Q3: distinguishing analytical inference from textual content
Q4: basic grammar, rubric and syntax, tenses
